boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's engagement at Maida (Santa Eufemia; 4 July 1806 by Bodart and Bunbury, the 5th by Koch) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1806 group: the British landing in the bay of St. Eufemia, Reynier's attack and the defeat and retreat of his division toward Catanzaro. The expedition's planning, the landing of 30 June and 1 July, the British return to Sicily and the risings in Calabria afterwards are context. Side A is the French. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side B (English and Neapolitans) 4,800 infantry under GM Sir J. Stuart and side A (French) 4,000 infantry and 300 cavalry, 4,300 men, under General of Division Reynier. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. His 4,800 for side B is Bunbury's 4795 rank and file who marched to the battle, rounded up (claim bunbury-side-b); the passages read do not show that he took it from Bunbury, and Bunbury's 20th Regiment landed during the action and is not in it. His figures for side A are below both other accounts: Koch gives Reynier's division 4,500 infantry and 300 chasseurs à cheval with a battery of light artillery (claim koch-side-a), Bunbury about 6300 in the action, including nearly 300 cavalry (claim bunbury-side-a). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'victory of the English and Neapolitans (4,800 infantry) under GM Sir J. Stuart over the French (4,000 infantry, 300 cavalry = 4,300 men) under General of Division Reynier'.

claims.value: Side A (French), its own account in Koch: when Reynier learned of the landing he gathered his troops and marched so fast that his division, 4,500 infantry, 300 chasseurs à cheval and a battery of light artillery strong, spent the night of the 3rd to the 4th in the wood of Fondaco del Fico; he resolved to attack despite the inferiority of his forces. The force included General Compère's brigade and a Swiss regiment, and the retreat was covered by General Franceschi with the 20e and the chasseurs of the 9e. Before the landing, Koch says, Reynier's small corps was split into countless mobile columns that no longer sufficed to put down the risings and keep open the communications with the capital (OCR).
claims.rationale: Side A's history, read from the page images except the mobile columns (OCR). The 4,500 and the 300 make 4,800 (our arithmetic). The parent OCR reads the infantry as 4,300; the page image reads 4,500. Reynier gathered what his dispersed corps could bring in time, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'hardly had Reynier been informed of it than he gathered his troops and marched with such diligence that his division, 4,500 infantry, 300 chasseurs à cheval and a battery of light artillery strong, spent the night of the 3rd to the 4th in the wood of Fondaco del Fico, from which it debouched on the 5th into the plain, by the road traced between the foot of the heights of Maida and the left bank of the Lamato'; 'he resolved to attack, despite the inferiority of his forces'; 'Reynier made his dispositions to attack the English line of battle in front, and ordered General Compère to cross the river with his brigade'; 'the Swiss regiment suffered a loss of 1,000 men killed and wounded'; 'the retreat was carried out in order by the heights of Tiriolo on Catanzaro, covered by General Franceschi with the 20th and the chasseurs of the 9th'; 'the small corps of Reynier, divided into countless mobile columns constantly on the move, no longer sufficed to put down the seditions and keep the communications with the capital open' (OCR).

claims.value: Side A (French) in Bunbury, the British account: before the expedition, spies and the court of Palermo put the enemy in Lower Calabria at no more than 5000 men under Reynier; on the 3rd reports of Reynier's strength were contradictory, some rating it at 6000 men, others at no more than 3000, and he was said to be awaiting the troops quartered at Reggio and other distant parts. In the field the enemy outnumbered the British considerably and had 300 cavalry, which the British lacked; his 1r Légère (three battalions) under Compère, supported by a regiment of Poles, the 42nd and, by his footnote on the enemy's right wing that faced Cole, '23 Legère, 3me battalions; Swiss 1 battalion'. Afterwards Bunbury writes that the British had about 5300 men in the field and the enemy considerably more than 6000, and that, by French returns he had held and lost, Reynier had 7300 men under his command, including the Poles at Monteleone and elsewhere but excluding the troops left at Scilla and Reggio, and, as he believes, about 6300 in the action, including nearly 300 cavalry.
claims.rationale: Side B's history on side A, read from the page images. Bunbury's 6300 rests on his memory of French returns he no longer had. His three battalions of the 1r Légère, against Koch's single brigade under Compère, are not reconciled in the passages read. The force was what Reynier's dispersed corps could gather, so the claim is tagged inherited.

claims.value: Reynier commanded side A and decided to fight. Koch: informed of the landing, Reynier gathered his troops and marched fast; whether because he believed, it is said, that he had found the chance of revenge on Stewart, who had beaten him in Egypt, or because the bands harassing his march made him fear for his communications with his magazines, he resolved to attack despite his inferior numbers; he made his dispositions to attack the English line in front and ordered Compère to cross the river with his brigade under cover of voltigeurs; Compère attacked without waiting for the rest of the division to come within support; a second attack was not supported by the rest of the army; Reynier's cavalry charges against the English batteries failed, and he ordered the retreat. Bunbury: Reynier reconnoitred the British positions on the 3rd with forty chasseurs à cheval; he handled his troops and opened the action in a masterly manner, but the French were too confident; surprised by the 20th, he drew off his troops skilfully (OCR) and retreated by the road to Catanzaro.
claims.rationale: Side A's decisions as both accounts give them, read from the page images except Bunbury's account of the drawing off (OCR). Reynier chose to attack, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): Koch, as in claim koch-side-a for the march and the resolve; 'whether Reynier, who had not been fortunate in Egypt in an encounter with Stewart, believed, it is said, that he had found the chance to take his revenge, or whether the bands that had harassed him during his march made him fear to see his communication with his magazines cut'; 'this movement is carried out hastily, and our voltigeurs are driven back by the enemy skirmishers; but soon Compère resumes the offensive and marches straight at the English without waiting for the rest of the division to be within reach to support him'; 'a second attack, which is not supported by the rest of the army, does not restore fortune'; 'in vain Reynier has several cavalry charges made against the English batteries; the battle is lost beyond recovery'; 'he then ordered the retreat'.

claims.value: Sir John Stuart commanded side B. Bunbury: Stuart took the resolution to make the attack on Calabria; on the 3rd he reconnoitred the French position and ordered the march at daylight on the 4th to attack the enemy's camp; in the action he seemed rather a spectator, formed no plan, declared no intention and scarcely gave an order (OCR), so Bunbury, then Quartermaster-General and acting head of the Adjutant-General's department (OCR), went round the brigade leaders himself (OCR); the most brilliant parts were Colonels Kempt's and Ross's, Kempt leading his light infantry forward to close with Compère's brigade and Ross's 20th, landed by a happy accident, attacking the French right; after the action Stuart ordered the army back to the beach (OCR). Koch: Stewart, timid or ignorant of the country, stayed at the foot of the hill of Santa Eufemia instead of cutting Reynier off at Nicastro or Catanzaro; seeing he was about to be attacked, he formed his troops with their backs to the sea, took the first fire standing still, unmasked his batteries and then advanced his lines.
claims.rationale: Side B's decisions as both accounts give them (page images except Bunbury's judgment of Stuart in the action, his own offices, his round of the brigades and the return to the beach, OCR). Bunbury, an interested participant critical of Stuart, credits the result to Kempt, Ross and the troops; Koch credits Stewart's use of his artillery and his advance. English renderings (ours): Koch, 'if General Stewart, who commanded this army, had been enterprising, he would have cut off Reynier's corps by establishing himself at once at Nicastro, or would have kept him from manoeuvring by the Adriatic coast by marching straight on Catanzaro'; 'whether from timidity or ignorance of the country, he stayed at the foot of the hill of Santa Eufemia, counting perhaps also on the news of his landing alone to complete the rising of the Calabrias'; 'Stewart, seeing that he was about to be attacked, formed his troops in line of battle, their backs to the sea, his right extended toward the mouth of the Lamato, and threw a strong chain of skirmishers into a small wood and the brushwood that shade the right bank of this torrent'; 'Stewart, standing still, takes the first fire, then, unmasking his batteries, soon wreaks havoc in our attacking columns, which are decimated before they can deploy'; 'the English general, profiting from the disorder his artillery causes in our ranks, advances his lines, and by this regular and bold movement increases the disorder'.

open_questions: Deferred: Stuart's despatch in the London Gazette, which Bunbury says was finished a fortnight after the battle, and the French returns he says he held and lost, neither inspected; French reports of the action, which the passages read do not cite; Koch's account of the sequel (OCR, cited only for Stewart's leaving the field), Bunbury's account of the 20th's attack, the pursuit and the march to Monteleone (OCR, cited in part), and his assessment of what might have followed (read and not cited). Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: Koch's date of Stewart's leaving the field, the strength of the Scilla garrison and Reynier's strength at Cassano afterwards; Bunbury's cavalry that might have destroyed the French and his estimate of the cavalry that could have been brought from Sicily; the page numbers of the OCR quotes.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength in the action and its loss. Bodart gives 4,000 infantry and 300 cavalry and a loss of 1,700; Koch gives 4,500 infantry, 300 chasseurs and a battery, and a loss of 1,000 in the Swiss regiment; Bunbury believes about 6300 were in action by returns he no longer had, and counts more than 500 French dead buried. The targeted follow-up read the headings and tables of Koch's pièces justificatives for the 1806 campaign in the parent OCR (n° II to n° XIV, pp. 400-428) for a return of Reynier's division in July 1806 and found none: n° III is the composition of the army on 21 February and n° IV an order of the day of 19 April printing an extract of the Moniteur. A French return for early July could narrow it.

Disputes recorded in the claims: the date (Bodart and Bunbury 4 July; Koch the 5th); side A's strength (Bodart 4,300; Koch 4,800 by our arithmetic; Bunbury about 6300 in action of 7300 under command); side B's strength and composition (Bodart 4,800 English and Neapolitan infantry; Koch 7,000 English and 3,000 Neapolitan or Sicilian troops embarked; Bunbury 4795 rank and file marching and about 5300 in the field, with no Neapolitan or Sicilian unit named); side A's loss (Bodart 1,700 with 1 general and 55 officers; Koch 1,000 killed and wounded in the Swiss regiment; Bunbury more than 500 dead buried, three-fourths of the 1st Légère); side B's loss (Bodart 350; Bunbury 326 killed and wounded by our arithmetic); the posture (Koch: the French attacked a British line formed to receive them on the beach; Bunbury: both armies advanced to attack in the plain); the British position (Koch: on the beach, backs to the sea; Bunbury: in the plain of Maida after a march along the shore).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his 4,800 for side B is Bunbury's 4795 rounded up, and his other figures are not in the passages read); Koch (the French history of 1850 from Masséna's papers and the war depot; second-hand for British figures); Bunbury (the British Quartermaster-General's narrative, written many years after the events, privately printed in 1849 and 1851 by its preface and published in 1854; critical of Stuart; his French figures from memory of lost returns). No passage read shows dependence between Koch and Bunbury.
